solution:
The molar mass in \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\) is numerically equal to the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula unit.

For \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\): \(2 \times 1.008 + 1 \times 16.00 = 2.016 + 16.00 = 18.016\)

Molar mass of \(\text{H}_2\text{O} = 18.02\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

The molar mass in \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\) is numerically equal to the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula unit.

For \(\text{CO}_2\): \(1 \times 12.011 + 2 \times 16.00 = 12.011 + 32.00 = 44.011\)

Molar mass of \(\text{CO}_2 = 44.01\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

The molar mass in \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\) is numerically equal to the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula unit.

For \(\text{CH}_4\): \(1 \times 12.011 + 4 \times 1.008 = 12.011 + 4.032 = 16.043\)

Molar mass of \(\text{CH}_4 = 16.04\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Mass per cent of an element \(= \dfrac{\text{mass of that element in the compound}}{\text{molar mass of the compound}} \times 100\)

Molar mass of \(\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 = 2(22.99) + 32.06 + 4(16.00) = 45.98 + 32.06 + 64.00 = 142.04\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Mass % of Na \(= \dfrac{45.98}{142.04} \times 100 = 32.37\%\)

Mass % of S \(= \dfrac{32.06}{142.04} \times 100 = 22.57\%\)

Mass % of O \(= \dfrac{64.00}{142.04} \times 100 = 45.06\%\)

(The three add to 100.00%, as they must.)

Na \(= 32.37\%\), S \(= 22.57\%\), O \(= 45.06\%\)

The empirical formula follows from the simplest whole-number mole ratio of the elements. Take \(100\,\text{g}\) of the oxide, so it contains \(69.9\,\text{g}\) Fe and \(30.1\,\text{g}\) O.

Moles of Fe \(= \dfrac{69.9}{55.85} = 1.252\)

Moles of O \(= \dfrac{30.1}{16.00} = 1.881\)

Divide by the smaller value \(1.252\):

Fe \(= 1.00\), O \(= \dfrac{1.881}{1.252} = 1.50\)

The ratio \(1 : 1.5\) is not whole, so multiply both by 2 to get \(\text{Fe} : \text{O} = 2 : 3\).

Empirical formula \(= \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\)

The balanced equation for the combustion of carbon is

\(\text{C}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g)\)

Burning in air means dioxygen is present in excess, so all the carbon is converted and carbon is the limiting reactant.

\(1\,\text{mol}\) C gives \(1\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{CO}_2\).

Mass of \(\text{CO}_2 = 1 \times 44\,\text{g mol}^{-1} = 44\,\text{g}\)

\(1\,\text{mol}\) (i.e. \(44\,\text{g}\)) of \(\text{CO}_2\)

\(\text{C}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g)\)

Moles of \(\text{O}_2\) supplied \(= \dfrac{16\,\text{g}}{32\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.5\,\text{mol}\)

The equation needs \(1\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{O}_2\) for every \(1\,\text{mol}\) C, but only \(0.5\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{O}_2\) is available against \(1\,\text{mol}\) C, so **dioxygen is the limiting reagent**.

Moles of \(\text{CO}_2 = 0.5\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of \(\text{CO}_2 = 0.5 \times 44 = 22\,\text{g}\)

\(0.5\,\text{mol}\) (i.e. \(22\,\text{g}\)) of \(\text{CO}_2\)

\(\text{C}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g)\)

Moles of \(\text{O}_2\) supplied \(= \dfrac{16\,\text{g}}{32\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.5\,\text{mol}\)

\(2\,\text{mol}\) of C would need \(2\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{O}_2\); only \(0.5\,\text{mol}\) is available, so **dioxygen is again the limiting reagent** and the extra carbon is left unreacted.

Moles of \(\text{CO}_2 = 0.5\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of \(\text{CO}_2 = 0.5 \times 44 = 22\,\text{g}\)

\(0.5\,\text{mol}\) (i.e. \(22\,\text{g}\)) of \(\text{CO}_2\)

Molarity \(= \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution in litres}}\), so moles of solute \(=\) molarity \(\times\) volume in litres.

Volume \(= 500\,\text{mL} = 0.500\,\text{L}\)

Moles of sodium acetate \(= 0.375\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times 0.500\,\text{L} = 0.1875\,\text{mol}\)

Mass \(= 0.1875\,\text{mol} \times 82.0245\,\text{g mol}^{-1} = 15.38\,\text{g}\)

Mass of \(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\) required \(= 15.38\,\text{g}\)

Concentration in moles per litre is the molarity, so work out the mass of \(\text{HNO}_3\) in exactly one litre of the sample.

Mass of \(1\,\text{L}\) of solution \(= 1000\,\text{mL} \times 1.41\,\text{g mL}^{-1} = 1410\,\text{g}\)

Mass of \(\text{HNO}_3\) in it \(= \dfrac{69}{100} \times 1410 = 972.9\,\text{g}\)

Molar mass of \(\text{HNO}_3 = 1.008 + 14.007 + 3(16.00) = 63.0\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Moles of \(\text{HNO}_3 = \dfrac{972.9}{63.0} = 15.44\,\text{mol}\)

Concentration \(= 15.44\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

The copper obtainable is the copper actually present, i.e. the mass per cent of Cu in \(\text{CuSO}_4\) applied to \(100\,\text{g}\).

Molar mass of \(\text{CuSO}_4 = 63.5 + 32.06 + 4(16.00) = 159.6\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Mass % of Cu \(= \dfrac{63.5}{159.6} \times 100 = 39.8\%\)

So \(100\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CuSO}_4\) contains

\(\dfrac{39.8}{100} \times 100 = 39.8\,\text{g}\) of copper.

Copper obtained \(= 39.8\,\text{g}\)

Take \(100\,\text{g}\) of the oxide: it contains \(69.9\,\text{g}\) Fe and \(30.1\,\text{g}\) O.

Moles of Fe \(= \dfrac{69.9}{55.85} = 1.252\); Moles of O \(= \dfrac{30.1}{16.00} = 1.881\)

Dividing by \(1.252\) gives \(\text{Fe} : \text{O} = 1 : 1.50\), and multiplying by 2 gives \(2 : 3\).

Empirical formula \(= \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\); empirical formula mass \(= 2(55.85) + 3(16.00) = 159.7\,\text{g}\).

The molecular formula is \(n \times\) (empirical formula), where \(n = \dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}\). No molar mass is given in the question, so \(n\) cannot be computed from the data; taking \(n = 1\) (the molar mass of this oxide is \(159.7\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)):

Molecular formula \(= \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\)
_note: The stem gives no molar mass, so strictly only the empirical formula is determinable; n = 1 is assumed. The book's own Ex 1.3 asks for the empirical formula from the identical data.

solution:
The average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of the isotopic masses:

Average atomic mass \(= \sum (\text{fractional abundance} \times \text{isotopic mass})\)

\(= \left(\dfrac{75.77}{100} \times 34.9689\right) + \left(\dfrac{24.23}{100} \times 36.9659\right)\)

\(= 26.4959 + 8.9568\)

\(= 35.4527\)

Average atomic mass of chlorine \(= 35.45\,\text{u}\)

One molecule of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\) contains 2 carbon atoms, so \(1\,\text{mol}\) of ethane contains \(2\,\text{mol}\) of carbon atoms.

Moles of carbon atoms \(= 3 \times 2 = 6\,\text{mol}\)

\(6\,\text{mol}\) of carbon atoms

One molecule of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\) contains 6 hydrogen atoms, so \(1\,\text{mol}\) of ethane contains \(6\,\text{mol}\) of hydrogen atoms.

Moles of hydrogen atoms \(= 3 \times 6 = 18\,\text{mol}\)

\(18\,\text{mol}\) of hydrogen atoms

One mole of any substance contains \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) entities (the Avogadro constant).

Number of molecules \(= 3\,\text{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 1.807 \times 10^{24}\)

\(1.807 \times 10^{24}\) molecules of ethane

Concentration in \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\) is the molarity, \(\dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution in litres}}\).

Molar mass of \(\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} = 12(12.011) + 22(1.008) + 11(16.00)\)
\(= 144.13 + 22.18 + 176.00 = 342.3\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Moles of sugar \(= \dfrac{20\,\text{g}}{342.3\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.0584\,\text{mol}\)

Molarity \(= \dfrac{0.0584\,\text{mol}}{2\,\text{L}} = 0.0292\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Concentration of sugar \(= 0.0292\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Find the moles of methanol needed, convert to mass, then use the density to get the volume of pure methanol.

Moles of methanol needed \(= 0.25\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times 2.5\,\text{L} = 0.625\,\text{mol}\)

Molar mass of \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH} = 12.011 + 4(1.008) + 16.00 = 32.04\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Mass of methanol \(= 0.625 \times 32.04 = 20.03\,\text{g} = 0.02003\,\text{kg}\)

Volume \(= \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{density}} = \dfrac{0.02003\,\text{kg}}{0.793\,\text{kg L}^{-1}} = 0.0253\,\text{L}\)

Volume of methanol needed \(= 0.0253\,\text{L} = 25.3\,\text{mL}\)

Pressure is force per unit area, and the force here is the weight of the air column, so \(P = \left(\dfrac{m}{A}\right) g\), where \(\dfrac{m}{A}\) is the given mass per unit area.

Convert to SI: \(1034\,\text{g cm}^{-2} = \dfrac{1.034\,\text{kg}}{10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}} = 1.034 \times 10^{4}\,\text{kg m}^{-2}\)

Taking \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\):

\(P = 1.034 \times 10^{4}\,\text{kg m}^{-2} \times 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2} = 1.013 \times 10^{5}\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}\)

Since \(1\,\text{Pa} = 1\,\text{N m}^{-2} = 1\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}\),

Pressure \(= 1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

The SI unit of mass is the **kilogram**, symbol \(\text{kg}\).

It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the Planck constant \(h\) to be \(6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\) when expressed in the unit \(\text{J s}\), which is equal to \(\text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-1}\), where the metre and the second are themselves defined in terms of the speed of light \(c\) and the caesium frequency \(\Delta \nu_{\text{Cs}}\).

SI unit of mass \(=\) kilogram (kg), defined by fixing \(h = 6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}\).

Each SI prefix stands for a fixed power of ten:

(i) micro \(\rightarrow 10^{-6}\)

(ii) deca \(\rightarrow 10\)

(iii) mega \(\rightarrow 10^{6}\)

(iv) giga \(\rightarrow 10^{9}\)

(v) femto \(\rightarrow 10^{-15}\)

Every experimental measurement carries some uncertainty, because of the limitation of the measuring instrument and of the person using it. That uncertainty is expressed by quoting the number of significant figures.

Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a measured or calculated quantity — all the digits that are known with certainty, plus one final digit that is estimated and therefore uncertain.

For example, in \(11.2\,\text{mL}\) the digits "11" are certain and the "2" is uncertain; the value has three significant figures, and an uncertainty of \(\pm 1\) in the last digit is understood unless stated otherwise.

\(1\,\text{ppm}\) by mass means 1 part of solute per \(10^{6}\) parts of the sample by mass, so

Mass fraction \(= \dfrac{15}{10^{6}}\)

Per cent by mass \(= \dfrac{15}{10^{6}} \times 100 = 15 \times 10^{-4} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\%\)

Per cent by mass of chloroform \(= 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\%\)

Molality \(= \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}\). Note it is per kg of SOLVENT, not of solution.

Take \(1000\,\text{g}\) of the water sample. At \(15\,\text{ppm}\) it contains

mass of \(\text{CHCl}_3 = \dfrac{15}{10^{6}} \times 1000\,\text{g} = 0.015\,\text{g}\)

Molar mass of \(\text{CHCl}_3 = 12.011 + 1.008 + 3(35.453) = 119.4\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Moles of \(\text{CHCl}_3 = \dfrac{0.015}{119.4} = 1.256 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of water \(= 1000 - 0.015 = 999.985\,\text{g} \approx 1.000\,\text{kg}\)

Molality \(= \dfrac{1.256 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol}}{1.000\,\text{kg}} = 1.26 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}\)

Molality of chloroform \(= 1.26 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

In scientific notation a number is written as \(N \times 10^{n}\) with \(1 \le N < 10\). Moving the decimal point three places to the right gives \(4.8\), so \(n = -3\).

\(0.0048 = 4.8 \times 10^{-3}\)

Write the number as \(N \times 10^{n}\) with \(1 \le N < 10\). Moving the decimal point five places to the left gives \(2.34\), so \(n = 5\).

\(234{,}000 = 2.34 \times 10^{5}\)

Write the number as \(N \times 10^{n}\) with \(1 \le N < 10\). Moving the decimal point three places to the left gives \(8.008\), so \(n = 3\).

\(8008 = 8.008 \times 10^{3}\)

Write the number as \(N \times 10^{n}\) with \(1 \le N < 10\). Moving the decimal point two places to the left gives \(5.000\); the trailing zeros are retained because they are significant in \(500.0\).

\(500.0 = 5.000 \times 10^{2}\)

The number already satisfies \(1 \le N < 10\), so the decimal point need not move and \(n = 0\).

\(6.0012 = 6.0012 \times 10^{0}\)

Zeros preceding the first non-zero digit are not significant — they only fix the position of the decimal point. So in \(0.0025\) the three zeros are not counted and only 2 and 5 are.

Number of significant figures \(= 2\)

All non-zero digits are significant, and a zero lying between two non-zero digits is also significant.

In \(208\), the digits 2, 0 and 8 all count.

Number of significant figures \(= 3\)

All non-zero digits are significant, and zeros between two non-zero digits are significant.

In \(5005\), the digits 5, 0, 0 and 5 all count.

Number of significant figures \(= 4\)

Zeros at the end of a number are significant only if there is a decimal point. \(126{,}000\) has no decimal point, so its three terminal zeros are not counted and only 1, 2 and 6 are.

Number of significant figures \(= 3\)

(If the value were meant to be known to more figures it would be written in scientific notation, e.g. \(1.26000 \times 10^{5}\) for six significant figures.)

Zeros at the end of a number ARE significant when they lie to the right of a decimal point. \(500.0\) carries a decimal point, so all four digits count.

Number of significant figures \(= 4\)

All non-zero digits are significant and zeros between non-zero digits are significant, so in \(2.0034\) the digits 2, 0, 0, 3 and 4 all count.

Number of significant figures \(= 5\)

Keep three significant figures: \(3\), \(4\) and \(2\). The first digit to be removed is \(1\), which is less than 5, so the preceding digit is left unchanged.

\(34.216 \rightarrow 34.2\)

Keep three significant figures: \(1\), \(0\) and \(4\). The first digit to be removed is \(1\), which is less than 5, so the preceding digit is left unchanged.

\(10.4107 \rightarrow 10.4\)

The leading zeros are not significant, so the first three significant figures are \(4\), \(5\) and \(9\). The first digit to be removed is \(7\), which is greater than 5, so the preceding digit \(9\) is increased by one, carrying into the \(5\).

\(0.04597 \rightarrow 0.0460\)

Keep three significant figures: \(2\), \(8\) and \(0\). The first digit to be removed is \(8\), which is greater than 5, so the preceding digit \(0\) is increased by one.

\(2808 \rightarrow 2810\), better written as \(2.81 \times 10^{3}\) so that the three significant figures are unambiguous.

Bring all four sets to a fixed mass of dinitrogen, say \(28\,\text{g}\), and compare the masses of dioxygen that combine with it:

(i) \(14\,\text{g N} : 16\,\text{g O} \rightarrow 28\,\text{g N} : 32\,\text{g O}\)

(ii) \(14\,\text{g N} : 32\,\text{g O} \rightarrow 28\,\text{g N} : 64\,\text{g O}\)

(iii) \(28\,\text{g N} : 32\,\text{g O}\)

(iv) \(28\,\text{g N} : 80\,\text{g O}\)

The masses of dioxygen are then \(32 : 64 : 32 : 80\), i.e. \(2 : 4 : 2 : 5\) — a ratio of simple whole numbers.

The data therefore obey the **law of multiple proportions**.

Statement: if two elements combine to form more than one compound, then the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other element are in the ratio of small whole numbers.

Distance \(=\) speed \(\times\) time.

Convert the time to SI: \(2.00\,\text{ns} = 2.00 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{s}\)

\(d = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1} \times 2.00 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{s}\)

\(= 6.0 \times 10^{-1}\,\text{m}\)

Distance covered \(= 0.60\,\text{m}\)

\(\text{A} + \text{B}_2 \rightarrow \text{AB}_2\) requires A and \(\text{B}_2\) in a \(1 : 1\) ratio; the reactant that runs out first is the limiting reagent.

300 atoms of A would need 300 molecules of \(\text{B}_2\), but only 200 are available.

So \(\text{B}_2\) is consumed completely and 100 atoms of A are left over.

Limiting reagent \(= \text{B}_2\)

The reaction \(\text{A} + \text{B}_2 \rightarrow \text{AB}_2\) needs A and \(\text{B}_2\) in a \(1 : 1\) mole ratio.

\(2\,\text{mol}\) A would need \(2\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{B}_2\), and \(3\,\text{mol}\) is available, so A runs out first and \(1\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{B}_2\) is left over.

Limiting reagent \(= \text{A}\)

The reaction needs A and \(\text{B}_2\) in a \(1 : 1\) ratio.

100 atoms of A require exactly 100 molecules of \(\text{B}_2\), and exactly 100 are supplied, so both are consumed completely and neither is left over.

There is no limiting reagent — the mixture is stoichiometric.

The reaction needs A and \(\text{B}_2\) in a \(1 : 1\) mole ratio.

\(5\,\text{mol}\) A would need \(5\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{B}_2\), but only \(2.5\,\text{mol}\) is available, so \(\text{B}_2\) runs out first and \(2.5\,\text{mol}\) of A is left over.

Limiting reagent \(= \text{B}_2\)

The reaction needs A and \(\text{B}_2\) in a \(1 : 1\) mole ratio.

\(2.5\,\text{mol}\) A would need \(2.5\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{B}_2\), and \(5\,\text{mol}\) is available, so A runs out first and \(2.5\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{B}_2\) is left over.

Limiting reagent \(= \text{A}\)

The equation must first be balanced:

\(\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3(g)\)

Moles of \(\text{N}_2 = \dfrac{2.00 \times 10^{3}\,\text{g}}{28.0\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 71.4\,\text{mol}\)

Moles of \(\text{H}_2 = \dfrac{1.00 \times 10^{3}\,\text{g}}{2.016\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 496\,\text{mol}\)

\(71.4\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{N}_2\) needs \(3 \times 71.4 = 214\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{H}_2\); since \(496\,\text{mol}\) is available, dihydrogen is in excess and **dinitrogen is the limiting reagent**.

(i) \(1\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{N}_2\) gives \(2\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{NH}_3\), so

moles of \(\text{NH}_3 = 2 \times 71.4 = 142.9\,\text{mol}\)

mass of \(\text{NH}_3 = 142.9 \times 17.0 = 2.43 \times 10^{3}\,\text{g}\)

(ii) Yes — dihydrogen remains unreacted.

(iii) \(\text{H}_2\) consumed \(= 214\,\text{mol} \times 2.016 = 432\,\text{g}\)

mass of \(\text{H}_2\) left \(= 1.00 \times 10^{3} - 432 = 5.68 \times 10^{2}\,\text{g}\)

(i) \(2.43 \times 10^{3}\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{NH}_3\); (ii) yes; (iii) dihydrogen, \(5.68 \times 10^{2}\,\text{g}\) remaining.
_note: The equation as printed in the stem is unbalanced (it shows N2 + H2 -> 2NH3). The balanced equation N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 is used, since no stoichiometric calculation is possible otherwise.

solution:
They are quantities of different kinds: one is an AMOUNT of substance, the other is a CONCENTRATION.

\(0.50\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\) states how much substance is present, irrespective of any solution. Since the molar mass of \(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\) is \(2(23) + 12 + 3(16) = 106\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), this is

\(0.50 \times 106 = 53\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\).

\(0.50\,\text{M}\) \(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\) states how concentrated a solution is: \(0.50\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\) dissolved in enough water to make \(1\,\text{L}\) of SOLUTION. The actual amount taken depends on the volume used — \(500\,\text{mL}\) of it would contain only \(0.25\,\text{mol}\).

So \(0.50\,\text{mol}\) is a fixed amount (\(53\,\text{g}\)); \(0.50\,\text{M}\) is a ratio of amount to volume of solution, and being volume-based it also changes slightly with temperature.

By Gay Lussac's law of gaseous volumes, gases react in volume ratios that are the same as the mole ratios of the balanced equation (at the same temperature and pressure).

\(2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\)

So the volume ratio is \(\text{H}_2 : \text{O}_2 : \text{H}_2\text{O} = 2 : 1 : 2\).

10 volumes of \(\text{H}_2\) require exactly 5 volumes of \(\text{O}_2\), which is what is supplied, so both are used up completely and

volume of water vapour \(= 10\) volumes.

The basic (SI) unit of length is the metre, and \(1\,\text{pm} = 10^{-12}\,\text{m}\).

\(28.7\,\text{pm} = 28.7 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{m}\)

\(= 2.87 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\)

The basic (SI) unit of length is the metre, and \(1\,\text{pm} = 10^{-12}\,\text{m}\).

\(15.15\,\text{pm} = 15.15 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{m}\)

\(= 1.515 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\)

The basic (SI) unit of mass is the kilogram, and \(1\,\text{mg} = 10^{-3}\,\text{g} = 10^{-6}\,\text{kg}\).

\(25365\,\text{mg} = 25365 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{kg}\)

\(= 2.5365 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{kg}\)

Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution, so a basis has to be chosen and the volume worked out.

Take \(1\,\text{mol}\) of solution in total. Then

\(n_{\text{ethanol}} = 0.040\,\text{mol}\) and \(n_{\text{water}} = 1 - 0.040 = 0.960\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of water \(= 0.960 \times 18.02 = 17.30\,\text{g}\)

With the density of water taken as \(1\,\text{g mL}^{-1}\), this water occupies \(17.30\,\text{mL}\); taking the volume of the dilute solution as essentially that of the water,

volume of solution \(= 17.30\,\text{mL} = 0.01730\,\text{L}\)

Molarity \(= \dfrac{0.040\,\text{mol}}{0.01730\,\text{L}} = 2.31\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Molarity of the ethanol solution \(= 2.31\,\text{M}\)
_note: The volume of the solution is taken equal to the volume of the water, which is what the stem's instruction to assume the density of water to be one licenses; no density is given for the mixture.

solution:
One mole of \(^{12}\text{C}\) atoms has a mass of exactly \(12\,\text{g}\) and contains \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) atoms.

Mass of one atom \(= \dfrac{12\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}\,\text{mol}^{-1}}\)

\(= 1.993 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{g}\)

Mass of one \(^{12}\text{C}\) atom \(= 1.993 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{g}\)

For multiplication and division, the result is reported with no more significant figures than the quantity having the fewest.

\(0.02856\) has 4 significant figures, \(298.15\) has 5, \(0.112\) has 3 and \(0.5785\) has 4.

The smallest of these is 3.

The answer should have **3 significant figures**.

For multiplication the result carries no more significant figures than the measured quantity having the fewest.

Here \(5\) is an exact (counting) number, and an exact number has an infinite number of significant figures, so it places no limit on the answer. The only measured quantity is \(5.364\), which has 4 significant figures.

The answer should have **4 significant figures**.
_note: The multiplier 5 is printed without a decimal point. If it were instead read as a measured value it would carry one significant figure and the answer would carry one; the exact-number reading is taken here, since a bare whole-number multiplier of this kind is an exact quantity.

solution:
For addition and subtraction the rule is about DECIMAL PLACES, not significant figures: the result cannot have more digits to the right of the decimal point than any of the numbers added.

Each of \(0.0125\), \(0.7864\) and \(0.0215\) has 4 decimal places, so the sum is quoted to 4 decimal places:

\(0.0125 + 0.7864 + 0.0215 = 0.8204\)

This result, \(0.8204\), carries **4 significant figures**.

The molar mass of naturally occurring argon is the abundance-weighted mean of its isotopic molar masses.

Molar mass \(= \sum (\text{fractional abundance} \times \text{isotopic molar mass})\)

\(= \left(\dfrac{0.337}{100} \times 35.96755\right) + \left(\dfrac{0.063}{100} \times 37.96272\right) + \left(\dfrac{99.600}{100} \times 39.9624\right)\)

\(= 0.12121 + 0.02392 + 39.80255\)

\(= 39.94768\)

Molar mass of naturally occurring argon \(= 39.948\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Argon is monatomic, so one mole of Ar contains \(N_A\) atoms.

Number of atoms \(= 52\,\text{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(= 3.131 \times 10^{25}\)

\(3.131 \times 10^{25}\) atoms of Ar

Here the amount is given in atomic mass units, not grams, so divide by the mass of ONE atom in u.

Atomic mass of He \(= 4\,\text{u}\), i.e. one He atom has a mass of \(4\,\text{u}\).

Number of atoms \(= \dfrac{52\,\text{u}}{4\,\text{u atom}^{-1}} = 13\)

13 atoms of He

Convert the mass to moles using the molar mass, then multiply by \(N_A\).

Molar mass of He \(= 4\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Moles of He \(= \dfrac{52\,\text{g}}{4\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 13\,\text{mol}\)

Number of atoms \(= 13 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 7.83 \times 10^{24}\)

\(7.83 \times 10^{24}\) atoms of He

All the carbon of the sample ends up as \(\text{CO}_2\) and all its hydrogen as \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), so the masses of C and H can be recovered from the combustion products.

Moles of \(\text{CO}_2 = \dfrac{3.38}{44.01} = 0.0768\,\text{mol}\), so moles of C \(= 0.0768\,\text{mol}\)

Moles of \(\text{H}_2\text{O} = \dfrac{0.690}{18.02} = 0.0383\,\text{mol}\), so moles of H \(= 2 \times 0.0383 = 0.0766\,\text{mol}\)

(i) Ratio \(\text{C} : \text{H} = 0.0768 : 0.0766 \approx 1 : 1\)

Empirical formula \(= \text{CH}\), empirical formula mass \(= 12.011 + 1.008 = 13.02\)

(ii) At STP the molar volume is \(22.7\,\text{L mol}^{-1}\), so

moles of gas in \(10.0\,\text{L} = \dfrac{10.0}{22.7} = 0.4405\,\text{mol}\)

Molar mass \(= \dfrac{11.6\,\text{g}}{0.4405\,\text{mol}} = 26.3\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

(iii) \(n = \dfrac{26.3}{13.02} = 2.02 \approx 2\)

Molecular formula \(= 2 \times \text{CH} = \text{C}_2\text{H}_2\) (ethyne, the usual welding gas)

(i) \(\text{CH}\); (ii) \(26.3\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); (iii) \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\)
_note: The molar volume at STP is taken as 22.7 L mol-1, the value this chapter itself uses. With the older 22.4 L mol-1 the molar mass comes out as 26.0 g mol-1 and the molecular formula is unchanged.

solution:
Work out the moles of HCl available, then use the \(1 : 2\) stoichiometry of the equation.

\(\text{CaCO}_3(s) + 2\,\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

Moles of HCl \(= 0.75\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times 0.025\,\text{L} = 0.01875\,\text{mol}\)

\(2\,\text{mol}\) HCl reacts with \(1\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{CaCO}_3\), so

moles of \(\text{CaCO}_3 = \dfrac{0.01875}{2} = 0.009375\,\text{mol}\)

Molar mass of \(\text{CaCO}_3 = 40.08 + 12.011 + 3(16.00) = 100.09\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Mass \(= 0.009375 \times 100.09 = 0.938\,\text{g}\)

Mass of \(\text{CaCO}_3\) required \(= 0.94\,\text{g}\)

From the balanced equation, \(1\,\text{mol}\) \(\text{MnO}_2\) reacts with \(4\,\text{mol}\) HCl.

Molar mass of \(\text{MnO}_2 = 54.94 + 2(16.00) = 86.94\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Moles of \(\text{MnO}_2 = \dfrac{5.0\,\text{g}}{86.94\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.0575\,\text{mol}\)

Moles of HCl \(= 4 \times 0.0575 = 0.230\,\text{mol}\)

Molar mass of HCl \(= 1.008 + 35.453 = 36.46\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Mass of HCl \(= 0.230 \times 36.46 = 8.39\,\text{g}\)

Mass of HCl reacting \(= 8.4\,\text{g}\)
